# Reliability

Reliability is the probability that a system of unreliable components is working. The structure function says which patterns of working components make the system work. Once the component states are random, the reliability function turns those patterns into a probability. Adding time turns the same function into a lifetime distribution.

Component lifetimes in this chapter are exponential, Weibull, or another law from [Random variables and distributions](prob-02-random-variables.qmd). The exponential and gamma formulas, means and variances are on the [common distributions](../reference/distributions.qmd) page. The Weibull law is not on that sheet, so it is recorded here.

## Structure

Each of $n$ components is either working or failed. Encode that by $x_i\in\{0,1\}$, with $x_i=1$ when component $i$ works. The system itself is working or failed, and in the model used here the system state is a function of the component states alone.

::: {#def-structure-function .definition}
## Structure function

The structure function $\varphi:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$ equals $1$ when the system works and $0$ when it has failed. A system is monotone when $\mathbf{x}\le\mathbf{y}$ implies $\varphi(\mathbf{x})\le\varphi(\mathbf{y})$: repairing a component cannot cause a failure.

:::

A series system works only when every component works, so $\varphi(\mathbf{x})=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i$. A parallel system works when at least one component works, so $\varphi(\mathbf{x})=1-\prod_{i=1}^n(1-x_i)$. A $k$-out-of-$n$ system works when at least $k$ components work, so $\varphi(\mathbf{x})=1$ if $\sum_i x_i\ge k$ and $0$ otherwise. Series is $n$-out-of-$n$. Parallel is $1$-out-of-$n$.

A system built by nesting series and parallel pieces can be reduced one module at a time. If component $1$ stands in series with a parallel module whose two branches are the series pairs $(x_2,x_3)$ and $(x_4,x_5)$, then

$$
\varphi(\mathbf{x})=x_1\bigl(1-(1-x_2 x_3)(1-x_4 x_5)\bigr).
$$

A bridge cannot be drawn as a pure series–parallel graph. Label the two side paths $1$–$4$ and $2$–$5$, and let $3$ be the cross link. Pivoting on the cross link splits the structure in two:

$$
\varphi(\mathbf{x})=x_3 z_1+(1-x_3)z_2.
$$

When the cross link works, the left side is joined to the right side, so $z_1=\bigl(1-(1-x_1)(1-x_2)\bigr)\bigl(1-(1-x_4)(1-x_5)\bigr)$. When it has failed, the two side paths are separate, so $z_2=1-(1-x_1 x_4)(1-x_2 x_5)$.

A minimal path set is a set of components whose working is enough to make the system work, and no proper subset is enough. A minimal cut set is a set whose failure is enough to make the system fail, and no proper subset is enough. For the bridge the minimal path sets are $\{1,4\}$, $\{2,5\}$, $\{1,3,5\}$ and $\{2,3,4\}$, and the minimal cut sets are $\{1,2\}$, $\{4,5\}$, $\{1,3,5\}$ and $\{2,3,4\}$.

If $P_1,\ldots,P_m$ are the minimal path sets and $K_1,\ldots,K_k$ the minimal cut sets of a monotone system, then

$$
\varphi(\mathbf{x})=1-\prod_{j=1}^m\Bigl(1-\prod_{i\in P_j} x_i\Bigr)
=\prod_{j=1}^k\Bigl(1-\prod_{i\in K_j}(1-x_i)\Bigr).
$$

The first expression says the system works when at least one minimal path is entirely working. The second says it works when every minimal cut still has a working component. Expanding either expression, and using $x_i^2=x_i$, produces a multilinear polynomial in the $x_i$.

## The reliability function

Now let the component state $X_i$ be random, with $\Pr(X_i=1)=p_i$ and $\Pr(X_i=0)=1-p_i$. The system works with probability $\Pr(\varphi(\mathbf{X})=1)=\E\varphi(\mathbf{X})$. In general this probability is not a function of the $p_i$ alone, because the components may be dependent. From here on the component states are assumed independent.

::: {#def-reliability-function .definition}
## Reliability function

Under independent component states, the reliability function is $r(\mathbf{p})=\Pr(\varphi(\mathbf{X})=1)$, a function of the vector $\mathbf{p}=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)$.

:::

Independence makes $r$ the structure polynomial with each $x_i$ replaced by $p_i$, but only after the polynomial has been written so that no $x_i$ appears to a power higher than one. Substituting into $\varphi(\mathbf{x})=\prod x_i$ is legal, and gives $r(\mathbf{p})=\prod p_i$ for a series system. For a parallel system, $r(\mathbf{p})=1-\prod(1-p_i)$. For a $k$-out-of-$n$ system with a common reliability $p$,

$$
r(p)=\sum_{i=k}^n \binom{n}{i} p^i(1-p)^{n-i},
$$

the upper tail of the binomial distribution. The algebraic expression for $r$ can look like $\varphi$, but the two functions have different domains: $\varphi$ eats binary vectors and $r$ eats probabilities.

For the bridge, expanding the path formula and reducing squares gives

\begin{align*}
r(\mathbf{p})
&= p_1 p_4+p_2 p_5+p_1 p_3 p_5+p_2 p_3 p_4 \\
&\quad -p_1 p_2 p_3 p_5-p_1 p_2 p_4 p_5-p_1 p_3 p_4 p_5-p_1 p_2 p_3 p_4 \\
&\quad -p_2 p_3 p_4 p_5+2 p_1 p_2 p_3 p_4 p_5.
\end{align*}

For a large system the exact polynomial can be out of reach. If $E_j$ is the event that every component in the minimal cut $K_j$ has failed, then $r(\mathbf{p})=1-\Pr(\bigcup_j E_j)$. Inclusion–exclusion expands the union. Truncating after the first term, $\sum_j \Pr(E_j)$, is the rare-event approximation, and it is accurate when every $p_i$ is close to $1$ and the cuts are unlikely.

## Lifetimes

Give each component a lifetime $T_i$ with distribution function $F_i$, and assume the lifetimes are independent. The component is working at time $t$ when $T_i>t$, so its reliability at time $t$ is $1-F_i(t)$. The system lifetime $T$ satisfies

$$
\Pr(T\le t)=1-r\bigl(1-F_1(t),\ldots,1-F_n(t)\bigr).
$$

A string of bulbs in series fails at the first bulb failure. If 20 bulbs have independent exponential lifetimes with mean 1000 hours, the rate of each bulb is $1/1000$, the minimum is exponential with rate $20/1000$, and the expected life of the string is 50 hours. That is the series formula $r(\mathbf{p})=\prod p_i$ with $p_i=e^{-t/1000}$.

## Hazard and the Weibull law

::: {#def-survival .definition}
## Survival function

The survival function of a lifetime $T$ with distribution function $F$ is $R(t)=\Pr(T>t)=1-F(t)$ for $t\ge 0$.

:::

For a non-negative random variable the expectation is the integral of the survival function, $\E T=\int_0^{\infty} R(t)\,\dd t$, when the integral exists. The argument is integration by parts, or Fubini's theorem applied to $\E T=\E\int_0^{T} 1\,\dd t=\int_0^{\infty}\Pr(T>t)\,\dd t$. The mean time to failure is this expectation.

::: {#def-hazard-rate .definition}
## Hazard rate

If $T$ has density $f$ and survival function $R$, the hazard rate is $h(t)=f(t)/R(t)$ for $t$ with $R(t)>0$.

:::

For small $\varepsilon>0$, $\Pr(T\in[t,t+\varepsilon]\given T>t)\approx \varepsilon\, h(t)$. The hazard is the instantaneous failure rate among components still alive at $t$. An increasing hazard is an ageing component. A decreasing hazard is one that becomes less prone to failure as time passes, which can happen when weak individuals fail early. The hazard determines the survival function:

$$
R(t)=\exp\Bigl(-\int_0^t h(u)\,\dd u\Bigr).
$$

The exponential distribution with rate $\lambda$ has constant hazard $\lambda$. Assuming an exponential lifetime is assuming that the component does not age. That is the same fact as the [memoryless property](prob-02-random-variables.qmd#thm-memoryless).

::: {#def-weibull-distribution .definition}
## Weibull distribution

A lifetime $T$ is Weibull with shape $\beta>0$ and rate $\lambda>0$ when its density is $\lambda\beta\,(\lambda t)^{\beta-1}\exp(-(\lambda t)^\beta)$ for $t>0$. The survival function is $\exp(-(\lambda t)^\beta)$, the distribution function is $1$ minus that survival function, and

$$
\E T=\frac{\Gamma(1+1/\beta)}{\lambda}.
$$

The shape $\beta=1$ is the exponential distribution with rate $\lambda$.

:::

The Weibull hazard is $h(t)=\lambda\beta(\lambda t)^{\beta-1}$. It increases when $\beta>1$ and decreases when $\beta<1$. Shape is the ageing parameter. Rate sets the time scale.

::: {.callout-note}
## Key idea
Write the binary function that says when the system works, reduce it to a multilinear polynomial, and under independence replace each component indicator by its reliability. Put survival probabilities in place of those reliabilities to get the lifetime of a system that is not repaired.
:::

## Exercises

::: {#ex-prob-series-parallel .exercise}
## Three components, one of them essential

Components 1, 2 and 3 fail independently with probability $0.1$ each. The system works when component 1 works and at least one of components 2 and 3 works. Find the probability that the system works.

[Solution](#sol-prob-series-parallel)

:::

::: {#ex-prob-k-out-of-n .exercise}
## Structure of a $k$-out-of-$n$ system

Write the structure function of a system that works if and only if at least $k$ of its $n$ components work.

:::

::: {#ex-prob-bridge-pivot .exercise}
## Pivoting the bridge

In the bridge with side paths $1$–$4$ and $2$–$5$ and cross link $3$, the structure function has the form $\varphi(\mathbf{x})=x_3 z_1+(1-x_3)z_2$. Find $z_1$ and $z_2$.

:::

::: {#ex-prob-bridge-paths .exercise}
## Paths and cuts of the bridge

The bridge has minimal path sets $\{1,4\}$, $\{2,5\}$, $\{1,3,5\}$ and $\{2,3,4\}$. Write the structure function by the path formula, and expand it far enough to see the four path monomials. Say how the same system is drawn as a series arrangement of parallel modules, and as a parallel arrangement of series modules, if components may be duplicated in the drawing.

:::

::: {#ex-prob-christmas-lights .exercise}
## A string of twenty bulbs

Twenty bulbs are wired in series, so the string fails when the first bulb fails. Each bulb's lifetime is exponential with expectation 1000 hours, and the lifetimes are independent. Find the distribution of the lifetime of the string, and its expectation.

:::

::: {#ex-prob-mttf-integral .exercise}
## Mean life as an integral of survival

Let $T\ge 0$ have survival function $R$. Show that $\E T=\int_0^{\infty} R(t)\,\dd t$, assuming the integral is finite.

:::

::: {#ex-prob-hazard-survival .exercise}
## Survival from the hazard

Let $T$ have density $f$, survival function $R$ and hazard $h=f/R$. Show that $R(t)=\exp\bigl(-\int_0^t h(u)\,\dd u\bigr)$ for $t\ge 0$.

:::
